modules.title: Collaboration workflows
modules.summary: Use issues, pull requests, discussions, notifications, wikis, gists, and GitHub flow to collaborate effectively.

lessons.title: Collaborate with issues, pull requests, reviews, and discussions
lessons.summary: Use issues, pull requests, code review, discussions, notifications, wikis, and gists for the right collaboration job.
learningObjectives: Describe how issues, pull requests, and discussions support collaboration
Explain pull request review and issue linking at a foundational level
Recognize when notifications, wikis, and gists help workflow management
lessons.explanation:
Collaboration on GitHub is a set of lanes, not one giant comment thread. **Issues** track work, bugs, ideas, and decisions that need follow-up. **Pull requests** propose changes from one branch to another, creating a focused place for discussion, review, checks, and merge decisions. **Discussions** are better for open-ended questions, announcements, and community conversation.

A strong pull request tells reviewers what changed and why. Reviewers can comment on specific lines, approve, request changes, or continue the discussion. Pull requests can link to issues so everyone sees that work is in progress, and some keywords can close an issue when the pull request merges.

Notifications keep collaboration manageable. Watching every repository can create noise, so teams choose subscriptions intentionally: participating conversations, releases, issues, pull requests, discussions, or all activity as needed.

Documentation and sharing tools round out collaboration. A **wiki** supports longer project documentation. A **gist** shares snippets or notes quickly. GitHub Pages is also a documentation and publishing option, but this slice focuses on repositories, issues, pull requests, discussions, notifications, wikis, and gists. The **Plan repository work with Issues, milestones, and Projects** lab covers more issue planning; the **Fork an open-source repository and contribute with a pull request** lab explores community contribution without making forks part of this lesson's core scope.

lessons.technicalExample:
A pull request body can link work clearly:

```markdown
## Summary
Updates checkout error message.

Closes #128

## Review notes
Please check the wording in `src/messages.ts`.
```

misconception.myth: Every conversation should be an issue.
misconception.reality: Use issues for trackable work, pull requests for proposed changes, and discussions for open-ended conversation.

lessons.examTakeaway: Scenario clues matter: bug or task means issue; proposed branch changes mean pull request; broad question means discussion; updates overload means notification settings.
lessons.recap: GitHub collaboration works best when teams choose the right lane: issues for work, pull requests for changes and review, discussions for open conversation, and notifications for awareness.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Think of issues as tickets, pull requests as inspected packages waiting at the loading dock, discussions as the town hall, and notifications as your personal inbox.
lessons.anotherExample: A maintainer creates a wiki page for installation steps, then shares a short troubleshooting command as a secret gist with a teammate.

lessons.title: GitHub flow end to end
lessons.summary: Follow the GitHub flow from branch to pull request, review, merge, and branch cleanup.
learningObjectives: Choose commands and GitHub actions that support a branch-based workflow
Identify where issues, reviews, and notifications fit into the flow
lessons.explanation:
The GitHub flow is a lightweight way to collaborate without making `main` chaotic. It works for code, docs, configuration, and many other text-based projects.

Start with an issue or task so the team understands the reason for change. Create a branch from the latest `main`, then make focused commits. Push the branch to GitHub and open a pull request. The pull request explains the change, links related issues, shows the diff, and gathers review. Reviewers comment, approve, or request changes. The author updates the branch until the team is satisfied and required checks or reviews pass. Then the pull request is merged into `main`, and the topic branch can usually be deleted.

This flow keeps the stable branch understandable while still encouraging frequent collaboration. It also creates a useful record: the issue explains the need, commits show incremental work, the pull request captures review, and the merge records the accepted change.

For practice, use the **Create a repository, branch, and pull request on GitHub** lab for the web flow and the **Clone, commit, push, and open a pull request with Git CLI** lab for the command-line flow.

terminology.definition: A branch-based workflow for proposing, reviewing, and merging changes.
A focused branch for one change.
Combining reviewed changes into the base branch.
An issue connected to a pull request for traceability.

lessons.businessScenario: Northwind Traders updates a checkout message. The support team opens an issue, a writer creates a branch, a reviewer comments on the wording, and the pull request merges after approval.
lessons.technicalExample:
A compact GitHub flow command sequence:

```bash
git pull
git switch -c docs/checkout-message
git add README.md
git commit -m "Clarify checkout message"
git push -u origin docs/checkout-message
```
Then open a pull request on GitHub, request review, address feedback, and merge.

misconception.myth: GitHub flow means everyone commits directly to `main` as quickly as possible.
misconception.reality: GitHub flow uses branches and pull requests so changes are proposed, reviewed, and merged intentionally.

lessons.examTakeaway: Watch for sequence questions: branch first, commit focused changes, push, open PR, review, update, merge, then delete the branch when appropriate.
lessons.recap: GitHub flow creates a safe path from idea to merged work: track the need, branch, commit, push, review in a pull request, merge, and clean up.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Think of `main` as the published recipe book. A branch is your test kitchen, a pull request is the tasting session, and merge is adding the approved recipe.
lessons.anotherExample: A legal team updates a policy page: issue for the request, branch for the edits, pull request for review, and merge after approval.
